title: Silence, Incense, and the First Four Trumpets
summary: When the Lamb opens the seventh seal, heaven falls silent for about half an hour. Seven angels receive trumpets, and an angel offers incense with the prayers of the saints at the golden altar, then hurls fire from the altar to the earth. The first four trumpets strike a third of the land, the sea, the fresh waters, and the lights of the sky, and an eagle cries woe over the three trumpets still to come.
story: The seals of chapter 6 have been opened, and the interlude of chapter 7 has shown God's people sealed and safe. The seventh seal does not bring a new catastrophe at once; it brings silence, and then a new series of seven, the trumpets. What sets the trumpets in motion is the prayers of God's people, the same prayers of the martyrs who cried how long in 6:10. The first four trumpets fall on the created world in partial measures, a third at a time, warning rather than destroying outright. The last three, announced as woes, will fall more directly on people in chapters 9 to 11.
historical:
The trumpet plagues are built from the story of Israel's exodus from Egypt more than from any single first-century event. Hail and fire recall the seventh plague (Exodus 9:23-25), water turned to blood the first (Exodus 7:20-21), and darkness the ninth (Exodus 10:21-23). For readers in the province of Asia, the sea and its ships were the arteries of the empire's wealth, and the burning mountain thrown into the sea may have evoked volcanic imagery; Vesuvius had buried Pompeii and Herculaneum in AD 79, an event that shook the Roman world, though the text does not name it and not every interpreter sees a link. Jeremiah 51:25 had already called Babylon a destroying mountain that God would make a burnt mountain, and some see that background here.

The interpretive schools read the trumpets differently. Preterists connect them with the calamities of the Jewish war and the Roman world in the first century. Historicists traditionally matched them to invasions that struck the Roman empire in later centuries. Futurists read them as literal judgments in a final period. Idealists read them as pictures of how God's judgment runs through history, calling people to repent.
cultural:
Trumpets in Israel summoned the people to worship and to war (Numbers 10:1-10), and the prophets used them to sound the alarm before the day of the LORD (Joel 2:1; Zephaniah 1:14-16). Seven trumpets blown by priests brought down the walls of Jericho (Joshua 6). Silence before God also has prophetic roots: “Be silent in the presence of the Lord GOD” is the call of Zephaniah 1:7 as the day of the LORD approaches, and Habakkuk 2:20 bids the whole earth be silent before him in his holy temple.

The golden altar of incense stood in the holy place of the tabernacle and temple, before the curtain (Exodus 30:1-10), and the priest burned incense there morning and evening, while the people prayed outside (Luke 1:9-10). Here the incense and the prayers rise together from the angel's hand. The same censer is then filled with fire from the altar and thrown to the earth, echoing Ezekiel 10:2, where burning coals are scattered over Jerusalem. Wormwood is a bitter plant; the prophets used it as a picture of the bitterness of judgment on idolatry (Jeremiah 9:15; 23:15), and Deuteronomy 29:18 uses it of a root of idolatry among the people.
literary: The seventh seal opens into the seven trumpets, a structure that many readers see as telescoping: each series of seven emerges from the last. Others see recapitulation, with the seals, trumpets, and bowls describing the same period from different angles and with rising intensity (the seals affect a fourth, the trumpets a third, the bowls everything). Both readings note that each series ends at the brink of the end. The trumpets fall in groups of four and three, like the seals: the first four strike land, sea, fresh water, and sky, the four regions of creation, and the eagle's threefold woe (8:13) sets apart the last three. The fraction a third, repeated twelve times in verses 7 to 12, marks the judgments as severe but partial. The scene at the altar (vv. 3-5) is the hinge: the trumpets are God's answer to his people's prayers.

outline.t: The seventh seal: silence in heaven and seven trumpets given
Incense, the prayers of the saints, and fire hurled to earth
First trumpet: hail and fire on the land
Second trumpet: a burning mountain in the sea
Third trumpet: the star Wormwood and the bitter waters
Fourth trumpet: a third of the lights darkened
An eagle cries woe over the three trumpets to come

doctrines.note: The prayers of the saints rise before God with the incense, and the answer comes back to the earth as fire. The prayers of ordinary believers, which seem to change nothing, are shown as part of how God acts in history.

The trumpets echo the plagues on Egypt. They are judgments on a world that serves other gods, and they are partial, striking a third, because their purpose includes warning and a call to repentance (9:20-21).

The judgments strike the land, sea, rivers, and sky, the regions God made and called good in Genesis 1. Human idolatry does not stay private; it involves the whole creation, which Paul says groans awaiting its freedom (Romans 8:19-22).

words.note: Sigē, silence. Used only twice in the New Testament. After the loud worship of chapters 4 to 7, the silence is striking. Interpreters see it as awe before judgment, as a pause so the prayers of the saints can be heard, or as the hush before God acts, as in Zephaniah 1:7.

Salpigx, trumpet. In the Bible a trumpet announces the presence of God (Exodus 19:16), gathers the people, sounds for battle, and signals the day of the LORD. In the New Testament it also sounds at Christ's return and the resurrection (1 Thessalonians 4:16; 1 Corinthians 15:52).

Proseuchē, prayer. The prayers of the saints appeared in 5:8 in golden bowls; here they are mingled with incense and offered on the altar. Revelation insists that the church's prayer is not wasted breath but part of the story of how God's kingdom comes.

Apsinthos, wormwood, a plant known for its bitter taste. It gives its name to the star. In the Old Testament wormwood is a picture of the bitterness that idolatry and injustice bring (Amos 5:7; Jeremiah 9:15).

christ: The chapter opens with the Lamb breaking the seventh seal, so the trumpets, like the seals, come from his hand. It then shows the prayers of God's people rising before the throne, and for Christians this depends on Christ's priestly work: Hebrews 7:25 says he always lives to intercede for those who come to God through him, and the New Testament teaches believers to pray in his name. The exodus pattern of the trumpets also points to him. The plagues on Egypt were the prelude to Israel's rescue, and Revelation presents Jesus as the Passover Lamb (5:6-9) whose death brings about a greater exodus, freeing a people from every nation. The judgments serve that rescue.

hard.q: Do the trumpets come after the seals in time, or do they describe the same events again?
hard.a:
Readers divide here, and the question shapes how the whole book is read. One view reads Revelation mainly in sequence: the seventh seal contains the seven trumpets, and the seventh trumpet contains the seven bowls, so the three series follow one another toward the end. Many futurists hold a version of this. Another view, going back at least to Victorinus of Pettau in the late third century, reads the series as recapitulation: seals, trumpets, and bowls cover the same span, each with greater intensity, and each ends at the final judgment (compare 6:12-17, 11:15-19, and 16:17-21). Idealists and many others favor this reading, noting that the sixth seal already looks like the end. Some combine the two, seeing progression and overlap together.

On either view the pattern is the same: judgments come in measured stages, God's people are protected, and the end is certain.

questions: Heaven falls silent before the trumpets sound. When have you found silence before God more fitting than words?
The trumpets are set in motion by the prayers of the saints. Do you pray as though your prayers matter to what God does in the world?
The judgments strike a third and not the whole. What does their measured, partial character suggest about God's purposes in judgment?
